overview.body:
**Xiuhtēcuhtli** ​(*xiuhtecuhtli*) — ‌Fire, Time, ‌Hearth · ​"Fire Lord" ​— the ​Aztec fire ​god, ​lord of ‌the hearth ​and of ​the year ‌— belongs ​to the ‌Nahuatl tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the domain ​"Fire, Time, ​Hearth". The ​name means ‌""Fire ​Lord" — ‌the Aztec ​fire god, ‌lord of ​the hearth ‌and of ​the ‌year"[^1].

Xiuhtēcuhtli ​is the ​Aztec fire ‌itself: first ‌and last ‌of the ​gods, the ​hearth ‌at the ​center of ​every home ‌and of ​the universe, ​and the ‌god ​whose great ‌ceremony — ​the drilling ​of the ​New Fire ​— restarted ‌time ‌itself every ​fifty-two years.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name ​as **Xiuhtēcuhtli** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[xiuhtecuhtli.com](https://punicodex.com/xiuhtecuhtli/). The ​original carries ‌both stress ​and vowel ​length, and ​exactly one ‌historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ‌the name ​in Tier ​1. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*xiuhtecuhtli* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
No indigenous ​written attestation ‌survives for ‌this name; ​**Xiuhtēcuhtli** is ​a scholarly transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the name ​means ""Fire Lord" ​— the ‌Aztec fire ​god, lord ‌of the ​hearth and of ‌the year"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form *xiuhtecuhtli* ​survives only ​because the early ​domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; ‌it is a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Xiuhtēcuhtli** recovers ‌the full ​diacritic detail ​of the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly in the ‌address bar. ​The original ​carries both ‌stress and ​vowel length, and ​exactly one ‌historically valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, which ‌places the name ​in Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**x** → **X** ​— Same
‌- **i** ‌→ **i** ​— Same
‌- **u** → ​**u** — ​Same
- ‌**h** → ‌**h** — ‌Same
- **t** ‌→ **t** ​— Same
‌- **e** ​→ **ē** ​— Long ē ​of tēcuhtli
‌- **c** ​→ **c** ​— Same
- ​**u** → ‌**u** — ​Same
- ​**h** → ​**h** — Same
‌- **t** ​→ **t** ‌— Same
​- **l** ‌→ **l** — ​Same
- ‌**i** → ‌**i** — ​Same

The ​project holds the ​domain **xiuhtecuhtli.com** ​(xiuhtecuhtli.com) as ‌the canonical ‌home of ​this name[^2].

domains.body:
Xiuhtēcuhtli ​is ‌the Aztec ‌fire ​itself: ​first and ​last ​of ​the gods, ‌the ​hearth ​at ‌the center ​of ‌every ​home and ‌of ​the ​universe, ​and the ​god ​whose ‌great ceremony ​— ‌the ​drilling of ‌the ​New ‌Fire ​— restarted ‌time ​itself ​every fifty-two ‌years.[^1]

‌### ‌The ​Hearth

The ​three ‌stones ​of every ​Aztec ‌kitchen ​— his ​throne ‌in ​every ‌house.

### ​The ​New ​Fire

Every ​52 ‌years, ‌all fires ​died ‌and ​one ​was drilled ‌anew ‌— ‌the cosmos ‌restarted.

​### ‌Huehueteotl

​"The Old ​God" ​— ‌his other ​name: ​the ​ancient of ‌days, ​wrinkled ​with ​a brazier ‌on ​his ‌back.

### ​The ‌Center

​The ‌axis mundi: ‌fire ​as ​the pillar ​between ​the ‌levels of ‌the ​world.

mythology.body:
Xiuhtēcuhtli's myths ​are the calendar's: ‌the fire that ‌must be renewed, ​and the darkness that ​waits if it ​is not.[^1]

### ​The Drilling of ​the New Fire ‌(The Cycle)

At ​the close of ​each 52-year cycle (xiuhmolpilli), ‌the Aztec world ​extinguished every flame: ‌households went dark, ​debts were settled, ‌and the priests ​climbed Huixachtlan — ​Hill of the Star ​— to watch ​for the Pleiades' ​midnight passage. On ‌a captive's chest ​the fire-priest drilled ‌the new flame; ​if it caught, ‌the runner carried it ​to the Templo ‌Mayor, and every ​hearth in the ‌empire was relit ​from it. If ​it failed, the ‌stars said, the sun ‌would not rise ‌— and the ​world would end ​in the dark.[^2]

‌### Huehueteotl, the ​Old One (The ​Elder)

Under his other ‌name he is ​the oldest thing ​in the cosmos: ‌Huehueteotl, the wrinkled ​god who carries ‌the brazier on ​his bent back, ​present before the suns. ​The Aztecs put ​him at the ‌center of the ‌universe's four directions ​— the fire-pillar ‌of the world ​— and every domestic ​hearth was his ‌shrine: the smallest ‌and the greatest ‌cult at once, ‌the god of ​the kitchen who ‌is also the god ​of the calendar.

​### What Fire ​Asks (The Nourishment)

‌The codices show ​his contract: fire ​feeds the world ​and feeds on ‌it. Offerings of copal, ​of the first ​fruits, and — ​in the empire's ‌hard logic — ​of the heart, ‌were given to ​the flame that gives ‌light, heat, and ​the year. Xiuhtēcuhtli's ‌priests performed the ‌fire-walking and the ​self-sacrifice by fire: ​the god who ​is the gift and ​the cost of ‌the gift, the ‌oldest bargain in ​the Americas.

meditation.body:
Xiuhtēcuhtli is ​the god ‌of the tending. ‌Civilizations, households, and ​marriages are ​all the same ​fire: it is ​not the ​lighting that matters ‌but the ​keeping, and the ​empire knew it ‌— 52 ​years of warmth, ‌one night of ​terror, and ‌the drill again. ​He asks ​the hearth's question, ​which is the ​oldest one ​there is: what, ‌in your house, ​are you ‌keeping alight — ​and what ‌would you do ​on the night ‌it goes ​out?

The last ‌New Fire was ​drilled in ​1507; the empire ‌never saw ‌the next. But ‌the hearth refused ​the conquest's ​arithmetic: the vigil-candle, ‌the copal, the ​kitchen's three ​stones — the ‌old god ​simply moved into ​smaller rooms. Fire, ‌of all ​the gods, was ‌the one nobody ​could convert.

​The drill and ​the chest ​are the two ‌halves of his ‌arithmetic: the ​fire that is ‌rubbed into being ​by hands, ​and the life ‌given to ‌keep it burning. ‌Modern ceremonies keep ‌the first ​and retire the ‌second, and the ​god, presumably, ​accepts the revision ​— the ‌hearth always preferred ​being fed by ​work anyway.

​His hill is ‌surrounded now by ​the largest ​city in the ​Americas, and ‌the suburb's kitchens ​still hold the ‌three stones. ​The old god ‌does not need ​the empire; ‌he never did. ‌He needs ​three stones and ​a flame — ​the world's ​most durable temple, ‌rebuilt nightly, everywhere, ‌by anyone ​who cooks.[^1]
